full_details: At the Theatre the king was home from Ireland and the power was gone. Burbage had been too loud all week, fighting Phillips's Bolingbroke. He would not hold the roll, and he would not have Garnish in his ear. You gave him the long line from memory. You told him, low, half the voice, and to watch it as from a gallery seat, as if it were happening to someone he was sorry for. He went again, quieter than you expected, and he sat on the bare boards. You heard your own line come back. Cowley had six lines as Aumerle and was afraid of each, and held the roll as if it might go off. Burbage said he would play a weak king as a strong man at being weak, and that he does it better than his cousin does winning. Phillips bowed. By eleven the hired men had left their dice and apples in the door. Edith pinned the king's sleeve while Burbage held the crown. Nick asked if he means it all, even the parts he is putting on. You said that is the part. A clove was in your cheek. Garnish put nothing in the margin. Kemp was not called. At two you played Fair Em, and brought no part-name home. At the Bell, Hobbins was nine days on the way. He took the letter of the last of August, still sealed, and gave you Anne's, written the Sunday after you left, and a parcel tied with a knot of great confidence. You read it in the yard and again by the taproom window. It answers a letter she has not yet had. You did not open the parcel. The sentence in your letter still says the back mends. You did not change it. You did not open the coffer.
one_sentence: You brought Burbage down to half a voice on the Welsh shore, and at the Bell you read Anne's letter.
title: Half the voice, and Anne's letter
